newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh says some Burma refugees accept food.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh says some Burma refugees accept food.

text.p: Bangladeshi officials said Burmese refugees in one of their two camps began accepting food rations on Thursday, partially easing a 10-day boycott over alleged forced repatriation.
"The refugees at Kutupalong camp received their rations on Thursday afternoon," said Ali Imam Majumder, deputy commissioner of Cox's Bazar district.
"But refugees at the other camp at Nayapara were still refusing to end their food strike. But we hope they will follow suit soon," he told Reuters.
The Burmese Moslems, known as Rohingyas, began a food boycott on July 21 as part of a protest against what they believe are attempts by Bangladesh to forcibly repatriate them.
Clashes between police and Rohingyas resisting deportation on July 20 left nearly 20 people injured, forcing authorities to postpone the repatriation from the Nayapara and Kutupalong camps.

The officials said they had repeatedly reassured the 21,000 refugees, the remnants of 250,000 Rohingyas who crossed into Bangladesh in early 1992 to escape alleged persecution by Burma's military junta, that Dhaka would not send anyone home against their will.
Government officials earlier on Thursday said that the Burmese refugees insisted they would not return home until their military-ruled country had achieved democracy.

"We are at a loss (about what to do) as the defiant Rohingya refugees appear quite stubborn on their precondition that they will go back home only if democracy is ushered in Myanmar (Burma)," a senior official said.

Another official, Qamrul Huda, the government's Relief and Repatriation Commissioner, said: "We will not force them to go, but Bangladesh cannot afford to give them permanent residence. Nor would Bangladesh be able to ensure Burma's return to democracy."
Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad told reporters in Dhaka on Thursday the Rohingyas must go back to their homeland sooner or later.
"It is not possible for us to allow them a permanent settlement on our land. This problem has to be addressed by the international community," he said.
Azad also rejected allegations made by the refugees and the UNHCR relief agency that Bangladesh was forcing the Rohingyas back to Burma.
"The government is sympathetically handling the situation. We hope the problem will be over soon," he said.
"They (refugees) are behaving strangely, apparently hoping that Bangladesh will be held responsible for any consequences," one government official in Cox's Bazar said earlier.
The refugees on Wednesday handed a list of demands to the government officials.
"They include permission for the Rohingyas in the refugee camps to stay in Bangladesh until democracy is restored in Myanmar (Burma)," one official said.
Van To Nguyen, UNHCR representative in Cox's Bazar, said on Wednesday night after visiting the camps with Huda and talking to militant refugee leaders that he saw no immediate solution to the crisis.
Cox's Bazaar borders west Burma's Arakan province, home of the Rohingyas.
